overview.body:
**Gunnr** (*gunnr*) ​— Valkyrie ‌of War · ‌Battle made ​divine — is ​the valkyrie ​whose name is ​her office: ​Old Norse *gunnr* ‌is the ​ordinary feminine noun ​for 'war, ‌battle', and the ​tradition sets ‌that noun on ​horseback among ‌Óðinn's choosers of ​the slain.[^1]

​Her attestations are ​few and ​uncommonly strong. The ​*Völuspá* seeress ‌sees her ​riding in Óðinn's ‌company — ​'Skuld held a ‌shield, and ​Skögul was with ‌her; Gunnr, ​Hildr, Göndul and ‌Geirskögul' — ​and Snorri, defining ​what a ‌valkyrie is, gives ‌her the ‌purest function-statement in ​the corpus: ​'Gunnr and Rota ‌and the ​youngest norn, who ​is called ‌Skuld, always ride ​to choose ​the slain and ‌to decide ​the fighting.'[^2] The ‌Skáldskaparmál þulur ​keep her in ​the metrical ​roll of valkyrie ​names, and ‌the same word ‌returns to ​poetry as the ‌common noun ​'battle' — the ​theonym and ‌the thing are ‌one word, ‌declined two ways.[^3]

‌PuniCodex restores ​the name as ‌**Gunnr** — ​identical to the ​ASCII input ​apart from the ‌capital, because ​normalized Old ​Norse writes no ​diacritic in ‌this name. The ​mechanical rule ​therefore places it ​in Tier ‌2: nothing distinctive ​is lost ‌in transit, a ​statement about ‌orthography and never ​about the ‌figure. The temple ‌is domain-less: ​the plain-ASCII gunnr.com ​is registered ​to a third ​party outside ‌the collection and ‌is watched ​for release.[^4]

sources.citation: Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. gunnr.
Völuspá 30 (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 36 and Skáldskaparmál þulur, ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Gunnr, valkyries.

the-name.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in normalized ‌Old Norse as ​**Gunnr** (nominative; ​the common ​noun declines *gunnr, ​gunnar*). It ​is not ‌a compound and ​needs no ​parsing: *gunnr* ‌is the ​inherited Germanic word ‌for war ​— Old ‌English *gūþ*, Old ​Saxon *gūđea*, ​Old High ​German *gund-* — ​and the ​valkyrie's name ‌is that noun ​personified.[^1] When ‌the Poetic ​Edda names a ‌rider Gunnr ​and skaldic ‌verse uses *gunnr* ​for the ‌battle itself, ​the tradition is ​declining one ‌word in ‌two registers: ‌the field and ​its chooser.[^2]

​The ASCII ‌form *gunnr* is ​not a ​modern compromise ‌but the medieval ​spelling itself; ​normalized Old ‌Norse carries no ​diacritic here. ‌The Unicode ​restoration **Gunnr** therefore ​differs from ​the input ​only by its ‌capital. Because ‌the restoration ​preserves nothing the ‌ASCII form ​loses — ​no diacritic, ‌no distinctive letter ‌— the ‌name is ‌classified Tier 2 ​by the ‌project's mechanical ​rule.

The letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

​- **g** ‌→ **G** — ​Same, capitalized
​- **u** ​→ **u** — ‌Same
- ​**n** → ​**n** — Same
​- **n** ‌→ **n** ​— Same
- ‌**r** → ​**r** — ‌Same

No ​form of the ‌name is ‌held as ​a domain: the ​plain-ASCII gunnr.com ​is registered ​outside the PuniCodex ‌collection and ‌is watched ​for release.

sources.citation: de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. gunnr.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. gunnr.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name ‌is **/ˈɡunːr̩/** ​— Old ​Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- **Gu-** ​— Voiced ‌velar stop ​[ɡ] as ​in English ‌*go*, and ​a short ‌close back ​[u], as in ‌*put*, held ​brief
- ​**-nnr** — ​The doubled ​dental nasal ​[nː], genuinely ‌long as the ​spelling demands, ‌closing on ​the syllabic ‌trill [r̩] ​of the ‌nominative ending, ​which carries its ‌own beat ​as in ​modern Icelandic

‌For the ‌modern speaker, ‌the closest ​approximation is: ​'GOON-ur' — short, ‌doubled-n, ending ​in the ​lightly sounded ‌nominative trill, ​as in ​Icelandic Gunnur.

‌Kindred and historical ​forms of ‌the name:

​- **Old ​Norse** — ​Gunnr, valkyrie; ​also gunnr, ‌the common noun ‌'war, battle'
​- **Old ‌English** — ​gūþ 'war', ​the everyday ‌battle-word of ‌Beowulf, the ‌same inherited noun[^2]
‌- **Old ​High German** ‌— gund-, ​the battle-element ​in names ​such as ‌Hildegund
- **Modern ​Icelandic** — ​Gunnur, the ​unbroken living ‌form as ​a woman's ​given name

​Gunnr is Tier ‌2 because ​the restoration ‌preserves nothing ​ASCII cannot: ‌five plain ​letters and ‌a capital. ‌The fame of ​the word ​— the ​whole North's ​name for ‌war — ‌vastly outruns ​its orthography.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. gunnr.

domains.body:
**Gunnr** ​is catalogued ‌under the ‌domain Valkyrie ​of War ​— ​and the ​lexicon's gloss ​'War' is ‌exact, because ​the ​name is ‌the domain: ​*gunnr* the ‌valkyrie and ​*gunnr* ‌the battle ​are a ​single word.[^1]

​### The ​Choice ​of the ‌Slain

Snorri ​assigns Gunnr, ‌with ​Rota and ‌the norn ​[[skuld|Skuld]], the ‌standing office ​of ‌riding to ​every battle ​to choose ‌who falls ‌and ‌to decide ​the fighting.[^2]

​### The ‌Award of ​Victory

​The same ‌passage gives ​the valkyries ​the double ‌prerogative: ​they allot ‌death to ​men and ​award victory ​— ​defeat and ‌triumph are ‌both theirs ​to deal.

‌### ​Óðinn's Company

​Völuspá ranks ‌her among ‌'Herjan's ladies' ‌— ‌the women ​of [[odinn|Óðinn]] ‌Herjan, the ​Father of ​Hosts ​— riding ‌armed and ​counted, not ​as ​omens but ‌as soldiers.[^3]

​### The ​Word Itself

​Her ‌domain survives ​in the ‌lexicon of ​poetry: *gunnr* ‌remained ​a live ‌poetic word ‌for battle, ​the material ​of ​kennings, long ​after the ‌valkyries' mythology ‌was set ​down.[^1]

Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 36, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Völuspá 30 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

symbols.body:
The ​corpus gives ‌Gunnr no ‌personal regalia ​— ​her iconography ​is the ​valkyrie's common ​kit, ‌and the ​tradition fixed ​that kit ‌early:[^1]

- ​**The ‌spear** — ​The chooser's ‌weapon: the ​stroke ​that kills ​and elects ​in one ​motion, ‌the valkyrie's ​attribute from ‌the picture ​stones ‌onward
- ​**The shield ‌of the ​company** ‌— Völuspá ​arms the ​riders: Skuld ‌holds a ‌shield ‌as Gunnr, ​Hildr, Göndul ​and Geirskögul ‌ride ​with her[^2]
​- **The ‌horse of ​the ​ride** — ‌The valkyries ​'ride the ‌earth' ​in the ​seeress's vision; ​the mount ​is ‌the office's ‌vehicle, the ​choice arriving ‌from ​above the ​melee
- ‌**The valr, ‌the chosen ‌slain** ‌— The ​harvest itself: ‌the dead ​lying ​on the ​field, selected ‌by name ​— ​the object ​her whole ‌mythology exists ​to ​gather
- ​**The noun ‌that is ​her ‌name** — ​The word ‌*gunnr* on ​a skald's ‌tongue, ‌meaning the ​battle and ​meaning the ​maiden ​at once: ‌the only ‌symbol she ​needs[^3]

sources.citation: Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. valkyries.
Völuspá 30 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. valkyries.

mythology.body:
Gunnr has ​no narrative of her ‌own; her mythology is ‌her office, and the ​sources state it with ​unusual unanimity. Three witnesses ​— the seeress's vision, ​Snorri's definition, and the ​skaldic name-lists — fix ‌her place in the ​cosmos.

### The Ride ​the Seeress Saw (Völuspá ‌30)

In the völva's ​great recitation, between creation ‌and Ragnarǫk, the valkyries ​appear as fixtures ‌of the world's order: ​'She saw valkyries come ​from far and wide, ​ready to ride to ​the gods' people; Skuld ​held a shield, and ‌Skögul was with her; ​Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul and ‌Geirskögul — now are ​counted Herjan's ladies, valkyries ‌ready to ride the ​earth.'[^1] Gunnr rides fourth-named ‌in the most famous ​catalogue of the ‌Poetic Edda, in the ​direct company of [[skuld|Skuld]], ​the norn of what ‌is owed. The company ‌matters: the seeress groups ‌the battle-choosers with the ​doom-weavers because the Norse ​mind treated the choice ‌of the slain and ​the decree of fate ​as one act.

### ‌The Choosers of the ​Slain (Gylfaginning 36)

Snorri, ​cataloguing [[odinn|Óðinn]]'s household, gives ‌the valkyries their ​definition and Gunnr her ‌single great sentence. Óðinn ​sends the valkyries to ​every battle; they allot ​death to men and ​award victory — 'and ‌Gunnr and Rota and ‌the youngest norn, who ​is called Skuld, always ‌ride to choose the ​slain and to decide ​the fighting.'[^2] It is ‌the purest job-description any ‌valkyrie receives in the ‌corpus: no genealogy, ‌no adventure, no death ​— only the perpetual ‌ride, present tense, always. ​Gunnr's myth is the ​claim that war is ​never random: someone rides ‌above it, and someone ​chooses.

### Kept in ​the Roll (Skáldskaparmál þulur)

​The þulur — the ‌metrical name-lists the skalds ​memorized as working vocabulary ​— preserve Gunnr among ​the heiti of ‌the valkyries, and the ​same poetic register hands ‌the word back as ​a common noun: *gunnr*, ‌'battle', fit matter for ​a kenning.[^3] The double ‌filing is the tradition's ‌own statement: when a ​skald sang of gunnr, ​his audience could hear ​the field or its ​chooser in the same ‌syllable, and no medieval ‌hand ever separated the ​two entries.

sources.citation: Völuspá 30 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 36, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur of valkyrie names, trans. Faulkes (1987).

syncretism.body:
Gunnr's truest ​kin are ‌internal. Snorri's ‌triad — ​Gunnr, Rota, ​and [[skuld|Skuld]], ​the youngest ​norn — ​binds the ‌valkyrie's battlefield ​choice to ​the norn's ‌decree of ​fate: two offices, ‌one act, ​the choosing ‌of who ​shall fall.[^1] ​The pairing ​is the ​Norse answer ​to a ‌question every ​warrior culture ‌asks: whether ​the dead of ‌a battle ​are taken ‌by chance, ​by doom, ‌or by ​someone.

The ​cognate record ‌shows what ‌did not ‌happen elsewhere. ​Old English ​kept the ‌same noun — ​*gūþ*, the ​ordinary battle-word ‌of Beowulf ​— but ​never grew ‌it a ​person; the ‌personification of ​war as ​a riding ​maiden is ​a specifically Norse ‌development.[^2] Comparatists ‌point to ​the Irish ‌battle-goddesses, the ​Morrígan and ​Badb, who ‌likewise decide ‌fights and ‌claim their ‌dead, as ​the closest ‌functional parallel ​in a neighbouring ​mythology; the ​resemblance is ‌real, the ​historical link ​unprovable, and ​the handbooks ‌rightly claim ​none.[^3] Within ​the corpus ​her closest ‌figures are ​[[freyja|Freyja]], who by ‌Snorri's account ​shares the ‌slain with ​Óðinn and ‌takes first ‌choice of ​her half, ​and the ​whole company ​of Völuspá ‌30 — ‌[[skuld|Skuld]] first ​among them.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 36, trans. Faulkes (1987).
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. gunnr.
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. valkyries, Morrígan.

cultural-legacy.body:
Gunnr's ​afterlife flows ‌through two ‌channels, the ​word and ​the ​image. The ​word never ​left the ‌North: *gunnr* ​lived ​on as ‌the battle-element ​of Scandinavian ‌naming — ​Gunnarr, 'the ‌warrior ​of battle', ​and Gunnhildr, ​'battle-fight' — ​and as ​the ‌living Icelandic ​and Faroese ‌women's name ​Gunnur, so ‌the ​valkyrie's name ‌is still ​spoken daily ‌by ordinary ​people ​who carry ‌it.[^1]

The ‌image is ‌larger than ​the ​name. The ‌armed maiden ​riding to ​the field ‌to ​choose the ​dead — ‌the figure ​Völuspá fixes ‌with Gunnr ​in ​the fourth ​seat — ​is the ‌seed of ‌the ​whole later ‌valkyrie: the ​walküre of ​the medieval ‌Germanic ‌revival, the ‌Valkyries of ‌Wagner's Ring, ​the shieldmaidens ‌of ​modern fiction ​and games, ​and the ‌valkyrie devotion ​of ​contemporary Heathen ​practice.[^2] In ‌scholarship she ​stands as ​the ​textbook case ‌of the ​Norse habit ‌of personifying ​powers: not ‌an ​allegory imposed ‌on war ‌after the ​fact, but ​war ​itself, declined ​in the ‌feminine and ‌given a ​horse.[^3]

archaeology.body:
No ​cult site, ‌votive deposit, ‌or ​named image ​of Gunnr ​is ​known; her ​attestation is ‌entirely ​literary, a ​silence she ‌shares ​with nearly ‌all the ​valkyries, ‌who were ​functions of ​Óðinn's ​household rather ​than objects ​of ‌cult.[^1]

The ​material record ‌knows ​the office ‌if not ​the ‌name. Gotlandic ​picture stones ‌repeatedly ​show a ​mounted warrior ‌received ‌by a ‌female figure ​bearing ​a drinking ‌horn — ​the ​so-called valkyrie-welcome ‌motif — ​and ​small armed ‌female figurines ​prove the ‌image's ​Viking-Age currency: ​above all ​the ​gilt-silver valkyrie ‌with sword ‌and ​shield found ‌at Hårby ​on ​Funen in ‌Denmark.[^2] The ‌textual ‌witnesses are ‌the Codex ​Regius ‌(GKS 2365 ​4to, c. ​1270) ​for Völuspá ‌and the ​principal ​Prose Edda ​manuscripts for ‌Gylfaginning ​and the ​þulur. The ​noun ‌*gunnr* itself ​is carved ‌in ​the runic ‌corpus, but ​within ‌personal names ‌— the ​battle-element ​of the ​anthroponymy — ​rather ‌than as ‌an invoked ​power.[^3]

meditation.body:
Gunnr ​is the ‌most ‌honest figure ​in ​the valkyrie ​roll ​because she ​pretends ‌to be ​nothing ​but what ‌she ​is. Other ‌choosers ​of the ‌slain ​carry names ​of ​tumult or ​of ​the spear; ‌hers ​is ‌the field ​itself. ‌To say ​that ‌Gunnr chooses ​the ‌slain is ​to ​say that ‌battle ‌chooses its ‌own ​— that ​once ‌the spears ​cross, ​the outcome ‌belongs ​to something ​no ‌combatant commands.[^1]

​The ‌Norse did ​not ​soften that ​thought; ​they dignified ‌it. ‌They gave ​the ‌blind lottery ​of ​combat a ‌rider, ‌a rank ‌among ‌Óðinn's women, ​and ‌a place ​in ​the seeress's ​vision, ‌as ​if to ​say: ​what you ‌cannot ​control, you ​can ​at least ‌name. ​Every soldier ‌who ​ever marched ‌out ​knowing the ‌choice ‌was not ​his ​own has ​stood, ​without knowing ‌it, ‌in Gunnr's ​shadow.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 36, trans. Faulkes (1987).

poetic-edda.body:
The Poetic ​Edda's witness ‌is a ‌single stanza, ​and it ​is the ​foundation of ​everything else. ​Völuspá 30 ‌sets Gunnr ​in the ​valkyrie company ‌the seeress ​sees riding ‌to the ​gods' people: ‌Skuld with ​her shield, ​Skögul beside ​her, 'Gunnr, ​Hildr, Göndul ​and Geirskögul ‌— now are ​counted Herjan's ‌ladies, valkyries ​ready to ‌ride the ​earth.'[^1] The ‌catalogue is ​not decoration; ‌in a ​poem that ​recounts the ‌making and ‌unmaking of ‌the world, ​the valkyries ​appear as ‌part of ​the world's ​standing machinery, ‌as fixed ​as the ​norms at ‌the well.

The ​names in ‌the stanza ​repay reading ​as a ​group. Several ​are plain ‌battle-words or ‌battle-titles — ​Gunnr 'war', ‌Hildr 'battle', ​Göndul 'wand-wielder', ​Geirskögul 'spear-Sköğul' ‌— and ‌scholars have ‌long noted ‌that the ​list reads ‌like the ​vocabulary of ​combat put ​on horseback.[^2] ‌Gunnr is the ​extreme case: ​not a ​word about ‌battle but ​the word ​*for* battle, ​the noun ‌itself among ​the riders. ‌The Edda's ​other valkyrie ‌lists — ​Grímnismál's roll ‌of cup-bearers ‌in Valhǫll ​— do ​not name ​her; her ​Eddic identity ‌belongs wholly ‌to the ​seeress's ride.[^3]

Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. valkyries.
Grímnismál 36 (Poetic Edda), the valkyrie roll, trans. Larrington (2014).

prose-edda.body:
The Prose ​Edda gives ‌Gunnr her ‌function and ​keeps her ​name. Gylfaginning ​36 is ​the defining passage: ​answering what ‌the valkyries ​are, Snorri ​says that ‌Óðinn sends ​them to ‌every battle, that ​they allot ‌death to ​men and ​award victory ​— 'and ​Gunnr and Rota ​and the ‌youngest norn, ​who is ‌called Skuld, ​always ride ‌to choose ​the slain and ‌to decide ​the fighting.'[^1] ‌The syntax ​deserves attention: ​the three ‌riders are ‌not an occasional ‌embassy but ​a standing ​patrol, present ‌tense, *jafnan*, ​always. Snorri ​binds the ‌valkyrie's choice to ​the norn's ​doom in ‌one clause, ​which is ‌as close ​as the corpus ​comes to ​a theology ​of battle.

‌The Skáldskaparmál ‌þulur then ​preserve her ‌in the working ​roll of ​valkyrie heiti ‌that every ‌skald memorized ‌— the ‌list-tradition by ​which the mythology ‌was transmitted ​as vocabulary.[^2] ​Between Gylfaginning's ​sentence and ‌the þulur's ​list, the ​Prose Edda holds ​everything medieval ‌Iceland thought ​worth keeping ​about Gunnr: ​what she ‌does, and that ​her name ‌belongs in ​the roll. ‌That the ​word also ‌served the ‌skalds as the ​plain noun ​'battle' is ​the completeness ​of the ‌record, not ‌a confusion ​in it.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 36, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur of valkyrie names, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. gunnr.

runic-evidence.body:
No ​runic inscription ‌invokes the ‌valkyrie ​Gunnr. No ​runestone asks ​her favour, ​no ​amulet bears ‌her name, ​and ​the silence ‌is expected: ​the ‌valkyries were ​functions of ‌Óðinn's ​household, not ​cult figures ​with dedicants.[^1]

​What ​the runic ‌corpus does ​preserve ‌is the ​word. The ‌battle-element ​gunn- runs ‌through the ​Germanic ‌name-pool — ​carved in ​the anthroponymy ‌of ‌the stones ‌in names ​built ​on *gunnr* ‌and its ​cognates, ​the same ‌element that ​surfaces ​in Gunnarr ‌and Gunnhildr ​— so ‌that ​the noun ​the valkyrie ​personifies ​has a ‌genuine epigraphic ‌life ​even where ‌the rider ​does ​not.[^2] A ‌normalized Younger ‌Futhark rendering ‌of ‌the name ​itself would ‌run ​ᚴᚢᚾᛦ (k-u-n-R): ​the k-rune ​writing ‌g, the ​single n-rune ​standing ​for the ‌geminate by ​runic convention, ​and ​ᛦ carrying ‌the final ​nominative ‌-r. No ​such carving ‌of ​the theonym ‌is known; ‌the ​rendering is ​a reconstruction, ​and the ​manuscript ‌spelling remains ‌the primary ​witness.

sources.citation: Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. valkyries.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. gunnr.

sagas.body:
The saga ​literature does ‌not give ‌Gunnr a ​scene, but ​it proves ​the world ​she belongs ​to. The ‌great prose ​witnesses to ​valkyrie belief ‌are famous ​set-pieces: Hákonarmál, ‌quoted in ​Heimskringla's saga ‌of Hákon ​the Good, ​stages Göndul ​and Skögul ​choosing the ​king on ‌the field of ​Fitjar and ‌escorting him ​to Valhǫll ‌— the ​office Snorri ‌assigns to ​Gunnr and ‌Rota, performed ​under other ​names.[^1] The ‌Darraðarljóð preserved ‌in Njáls ‌saga goes ​further, showing ​the valkyries ‌at the ​Battle of ​Clontarf in ‌1014 weaving ​men's fates ​with guts ‌for warp and ​heads for ‌loom-weights: the ​grimmest surviving ​picture of ​battle-choice as ​a textile ‌of doom.[^2]

‌Gunnr is ​named in ‌neither poem, ​and the ​record should ‌not pretend ‌otherwise. What ‌the sagas ‌establish is ​the milieu: ‌a literary ​culture, Christian ​for two ​centuries, that ‌still found the ​chooser of ​the slain ​its most ‌natural language ​for what ​battle does ​to men. ‌The triad ​Snorri names ‌— Gunnr, ​Rota, and ‌[[skuld|Skuld]] — ​is the ‌doctrine; the ‌saga poems ​are its ​practice, witnessed ​in the ​work of ‌named poets ‌writing for ​named kings.[^3]

sources.citation: Eyvindr skáldaspillir, Hákonarmál, quoted in Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Hákonar saga góða, trans. Lee M. Hollander (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1964).
Darraðarljóð, in Brennu-Njáls saga ch. 157, trans. Robert Cook, Njal's Saga (London: Penguin, 2001).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 36, trans. Faulkes (1987).

original-script.body:
The name ​is preserved ‌in medieval ‌Icelandic manuscripts ​in the ​Latin alphabet ​as **Gunnr** ​— Old ​Norse (North ‌Germanic), attested ​13th c. ​CE in ‌the Codex ​Regius of ‌the Poetic ​Edda (Völuspá 30) ‌and in ​the principal ​codices of ​the Prose ​Edda, recording ​material centuries ‌older.[^1] Before ​the Latin ‌bookhand, Old ​Norse names ‌were carved ​in the ‌Younger Futhark; ​no runic attestation ‌of this ​valkyrie-name survives, ​so the ‌manuscript form ‌is the ‌primary witness.

​The scholarly ​rendering proceeds ‌step by ​step:

- ​The name ‌is the ​common noun ​*gunnr*, feminine, ‌'war, battle', with ​the nominative ‌singular ending ​*-r*.
- ​Old Norse ​orthography marks ​no diacritic ‌in this ‌word: vowel ​u is ‌short, and ​the doubled ​nn writes ‌a genuinely ‌long consonant.
‌- In the ‌Younger Futhark ​the name ‌would have ​been carved ​ᚴᚢᚾᛦ (k-u-n-R), ​the k-rune ‌writing g, ​a single ​n-rune for ​the geminate, ‌and ᛦ ​the nominative ​-r.
- ​The Unicode restoration ‌Gunnr is ​therefore identical ‌to the ​ASCII form ‌apart from ​the capital: ‌the manuscripts ‌themselves write ​plain ASCII, ​and the ​restoration is ​a matter ‌of canonical ‌reference, not ​rescued letters.[^2]

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957).
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. gunnr.
